Prepared consistent preprocessing and a reusable class index mapping. Documented data quality checks and potential sources of bias.

title: Proposal
content:
AWS Plant Disease Detection Project Proposal Twelve week implementation and validation plan 16 October 2026 | Sydney | ap-southeast-2
We propose a twelve-week implementation and validation program for a containerized tomato leaf classification application on EC2, S3 and CloudWatch. The plan starts from the existing prototype and closes deployment, evidence and operational gaps.
1 Executive summary The project will deliver a reproducible AWS demonstration with a responsive frontend, CPU inference API, privately stored model artifacts and one operational RAM alarm. GitHub Actions will publish images; a controlled manual procedure will deploy and roll back compatible image and model versions. This scope fits a backend and MLOps learning project without requiring serverless or microservices claims.
The planning scenario uses 240 EC2 hours over twelve weeks and a gross budget of USD 67.20 including a 20 percent contingency. The account screenshot showed USD 100 available; an additional USD 100 is not assumed to be earned. Actual credit eligibility, expiry, regional prices and tax must be checked before spending. The estimate is a planning allowance, not an AWS quotation. [6–12]
2 Problem statement A locally trained classifier is difficult to reproduce on another host when model weights, class ordering, preprocessing and dependencies are managed separately. LAN-only access limits demonstrations, and an apparently healthy process may still fail prediction because of missing weights, CORS, queue saturation or permission errors. Source-code synchronization alone does not update a running container.
The project therefore needs a versioned release identity, least-privilege access to artifacts, evidence of real inference on AWS, actionable host monitoring and a documented recovery process. The current prototype supplies working components, but it does not yet establish high availability, field accuracy or automated production deployment.
3 Solution architecture AWS services used Service Role Design choice Amazon EC2 Run frontend and API containers One x86_64 host in Sydney Amazon S3 Store checkpoint and class map Private versioned artifacts Amazon CloudWatch Logs metrics dashboard and RAM alarm 60 second Agent metrics; 7 day logs IAM and VPC Identity and network controls Instance role and source IP rules Amazon SNS Deliver alarm email One confirmed email subscription Component design The browser reaches Next.js on port 3000 and FastAPI on port 8000 at the same EC2 hostname. FastAPI loads a MobileNet checkpoint once per process and validates the supplied class map. Prediction and Grad-CAM++ share a bounded execution slot. S3 is accessed at deployment time; uploaded user images do not need to be persisted in S3 for the current use case.
GitHub Actions -> GHCR -> manual deployment to EC2 Private S3 artifacts -> host version directory -> read-only API mount Browser -> Next.js frontend and FastAPI API Container logs + Agent metrics -> CloudWatch -> RAM alarm -> SNS The architecture deliberately uses a public subnet with restricted inbound access for the demonstration. S3 VPC endpoints, on-premises connectivity, DNS simulation, load balancing and autoscaling are outside the baseline. A private-network extension can be evaluated later without being reported as an implemented feature.
4 Technical implementation Build the frontend with its existing multi-stage Dockerfile and standalone Next.js output. Build the API with Dockerfile.deploy so the checkpoint remains outside the image. CI gates include Python tests, frontend build, backend build and frontend container smoke tests. Publish both images with full commit tags and record digests; tests using fixture weights remain distinct from real-model acceptance tests.
Create the EC2 instance profile with scoped GetObject permission and CloudWatch delivery permissions. Download model artifacts from mobilenet-distilled-v1 and compare SHA256 values before mounting them read-only. Bind the API and frontend ports, configure CORS_ORIGINS with the exact page origin and use restart unless-stopped. Recreate containers when changing image or environment settings.
Validate readiness, real-image prediction, response schema and model identity. Then validate browser upload and Grad-CAM++ on desktop and phone. Measure API latency under a declared request count and concurrency instead of interpreting a single request as p95. Evaluate macro F1 and per-class recall only when an independent labeled dataset is available; do not promise a diagnostic accuracy without that evaluation.
Use CloudWatch Logs for both containers and Agent metrics for RAM and disk. Retain logs for seven days and configure one RAM alarm at Average greater than 85 percent for three one-minute datapoints. Confirm SNS delivery with a controlled threshold test, then restore 85. Record rollback and EC2 stop/start rehearsals, including public IP and CORS updates.
5 Timelines and milestones Each week receives 20 planned working hours, totaling 240 hours. This is a proposed twelve-week schedule, not a reconstruction of dates already worked. EC2 runtime is separately capped at a planning total of 240 hours; it need not match every working hour.
Week Work package Milestone evidence 1 20 h Scope and acceptance criteria Architecture scope agreed 2 20 h Audit model preprocessing and labels Artifact manifest and hashes 3 20 h Harden API validation and errors API contract and tests 4 20 h Validate frontend and explanations Browser workflow verified locally 5 20 h Package production containers Two images pass smoke tests 6 20 h Complete CI and GHCR delivery Published release digests 7 20 h Prepare AWS IAM network and budget EC2 role and restricted connectivity 8 20 h Store and retrieve S3 artifacts Download hashes match 9 20 h Deploy EC2 and test real inference Desktop and phone acceptance 10 20 h Configure CloudWatch and RAM alarm Metrics logs and email test 11 20 h Rehearse rollback and measure latency Recovery and performance evidence 12 20 h Finalize report demo and cleanup Handover and cost review 6 Budget estimation Budget in USD before tax, credits and discounts, for Sydney. Assume one c7i-flex.large or another approved x86_64 instance only after checking availability and price. The existing instance type has not been verified. The EC2 allowance of USD 0.12 per hour and gp3 allowance of USD 0.12 per GiB-month are deliberately rounded planning inputs, not claimed Sydney list prices. Recalculate if the selected type exceeds the allowance. Public IPv4 uses the published USD 0.005 per hour rate. [6–8]
Item Basis USD EC2 240 h × $0.12 $28.80 Public IPv4 240 h × $0.005 $1.20 EBS gp3 30 GiB × 3 months × $0.12 $10.80 CloudWatch metrics dashboard alarm $3/month allowance × 3 $9.00 CloudWatch Logs and queries $1/month allowance × 3 $3.00 S3 storage versions requests Project allowance $1.00 SNS email Project allowance $0.20 Data transfer Low-traffic allowance $2.00 Subtotal $56.00 Contingency 20% × $56.00 $11.20 Total $67.20 The twelve weeks span 84 days; storage and fixed monitoring allowances are rounded up to three months. CloudWatch and S3 amounts are spending envelopes, not exact unit-rate calculations, and do not rely on Free Tier exemptions. The transfer allowance is suitable only for a small demonstration. Taxes, domain purchase, load balancers, NAT Gateway, GPUs, model training and extra VPC endpoints are excluded. [7–10]
At the same assumptions, leaving EC2 and its public IPv4 running for all 2,016 hours of twelve weeks raises the subtotal to USD 278.00 and the total with contingency to USD 333.60. Scheduled manual stops are therefore essential for this credit-limited plan. EBS and retained monitoring resources still cost money while the instance is stopped. [2,6–9]
Use only the verified USD 100 credit balance until additional credit is actually granted. The planned gross estimate leaves USD 32.80 headroom before actual pricing differences and tax. Configure a monthly budget alert and review actual gross usage weekly with credits excluded from the view. Budget notifications are not an immediate hard spending cap. [11–12]
7 Risk assessment Risk Likelihood and impact Mitigation and owner Credit depletion Medium / High Operator stops EC2 and reviews gross costs weekly Instance capacity or plan restriction Medium / Medium Operator checks eligible x86_64 type and revises budget Incorrect model or class order Medium / High ML developer verifies hashes map and preprocessing CORS or public IP change High / Medium Backend operator recreates container with correct origin Access or credential exposure Medium / High Operator uses instance role private S3 and restricted SSH Host outage or saturation Medium / High Backend operator measures queue load and rehearses recovery Alarm email not delivered Medium / Medium Operator confirms SNS and performs threshold test Field data differs from training High / High ML developer collects labeled samples and limits claims The initial demonstrator accepts single-host downtime and HTTP access restricted to approved client IPs. Public production use requires a separate security and availability review, including HTTPS and authentication. The RAM alarm is intentionally the only operational alarm in this scope and does not cover service availability or ML quality.
8 Expected outcomes Outcome Acceptance evidence Reproducible release Two image digests plus checkpoint map hashes and config Working AWS application Health and prediction succeed; browser prediction and explanation verified Secure artifact retrieval Private S3 GetObject by instance role with matching hashes Operational visibility Logs host dashboard one RAM alarm and a received SNS email Documented recovery Rollback and EC2 stop/start rehearsal with observed timings Measured performance Latency report states image hardware concurrency samples and p95 Controlled cost Weekly gross-cost log and final cleanup evidence Success means a demonstrable and documented deployment within the approved spending envelope. It does not mean a proven agricultural diagnosis service, a zero-downtime platform or a completed twelve-week historical project. Accuracy and recovery objectives will be reported only after measurement.
References AWS documentation and pricing references accessed on 16 October 2026. Usage allowances in the proposal are planning assumptions, not a regional price quotation.

title: Week 2 Worklog
content:
Week 02 Worklog - Model Training and Artifact Preparation Project: Tomato leaf disease detection on AWS
Period: Week 02 working days 1 to 5
Week Objectives: Train and review a lightweight tomato leaf classifier. Prepare model files suitable for CPU inference on Amazon EC2. Record model identity without relying on unsupported accuracy claims. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 1 Review the MobileNetV3 Small configuration and initialize the training environment. Check that model output dimensions match the class index mapping. W02 D1 W02 D1 Project dataset and model notes 2 Run an initial training experiment. Review training and validation loss to identify configuration errors and signs of overfitting. W02 D2 W02 D2 Project dataset and model notes 3 Review the lightweight student model and knowledge distillation workflow. Compare candidate checkpoints using the same validation partition and preprocessing. W02 D3 W02 D3 Project dataset and model notes 4 Evaluate the selected checkpoint on held-out images. Inspect class-level errors and verify CPU inference with the matching class mapping. W02 D4 W02 D4 Project dataset and model notes 5 Export the selected checkpoint as model.pth and the label mapping as class_to_idx.json. Calculate SHA256 hashes for later cloud integrity checks. W02 D5 W02 D5 Project dataset and model notes Achievements: Prepared a lightweight model checkpoint and compatible class mapping. Reviewed model behavior and CPU inference before cloud deployment. Created identifiable artifacts for storage and retrieval on Amazon S3.

title: Workshop
content:
AWS Deployment Workshop Report Tomato Leaf Disease Classification with EC2, S3, and CloudWatch Region: Asia Pacific (Sydney) ap-southeast-2
Source Repository: starkkk1/plant-disease-detection
Deployment Status: Containerized Production Demonstration on AWS
Executive Summary The Plant Disease Detection project has successfully progressed from local PyTorch research to a containerized, production-grade cloud deployment on Amazon Web Services (AWS).
A single Amazon EC2 instance hosts a responsive Next.js web frontend and a high-performance FastAPI CPU inference service. Amazon S3 provides secure, decoupled storage for versioned deep learning model weights, while Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon SNS collect real-time operational telemetry, host metrics, and dispatch proactive memory saturation alarms.
Recorded Configuration Configuration Item Recorded Specification AWS Region Asia Pacific Sydney / ap-southeast-2 Primary AWS Services Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch Supporting Services AWS IAM, Amazon VPC, Security Groups, Amazon SNS Application Stack Next.js Standalone (Node.js 20), FastAPI, PyTorch (CPU), Docker, GHCR Deployment Model Single host with dual isolated containers; manual release promotion Machine Learning Architecture Knowledge-distilled MobileNetV3-Small (Student) from ConvNeXt-Tiny (Teacher) Monitoring Scope Custom CloudWatch Agent (CPU, RAM, Disk metrics) + Automated RAM Alarm (>85%) End-to-End Operational Pipeline flowchart LR Dev[Developer / Git Push] --> GHA[GitHub Actions CI/CD] GHA -->|Build & Test| GHCR[GitHub Packages / GHCR] subgraph AWS_Cloud ["AWS Cloud (ap-southeast-2)"] subgraph EC2_Host ["Amazon EC2 Instance"] FE["Next.js Frontend Container (:3000)"] BE["FastAPI Backend Container (:8000)"] CW_Agent["CloudWatch Agent (Host Metrics)"] FE -->|Inference Call| BE end S3["Amazon S3 Bucket (Private Checkpoints)"] -->|Mount Read-Only| BE BE -->|stdout / stderr| CW_Logs["CloudWatch Logs (/plant-disease)"] CW_Agent -->|mem_used_percent| CW_Alarm["CloudWatch RAM Alarm (>85%)"] CW_Alarm -->|Trigger| SNS["Amazon SNS Topic (Email Alert)"] end GHCR -->|Deploy Images| EC2_Host Client["User Mobile / Desktop Browser"] -->|HTTP :3000| FE Workshop Sections 5.1 Introduction Introduction to the 11-class tomato leaf classification problem, knowledge distillation benchmarks, and Grad-CAM++ explainability. 5.2 Prerequisites & Setup AWS account configuration, VPC subnets, client-restricted Security Groups, IAM Instance Profiles, and Docker engine setup. 5.3 Architecture & Design Decoupled model artifact architecture, S3 bucket security, IAM assumed-role validation, and SHA256 integrity verification. 5.4 Deployment Strategy Multi-stage Docker builds, runtime environment configuration, Next.js standalone serving, and live inference validation with real leaf fixtures. 5.5 Testing & Quality Structured JSON container logging with AWSlogs driver, CloudWatch Agent memory telemetry, automated RAM breach alarms, and least-privilege security. 5.6 Operations & Cleanup Daily container start/stop procedures, dynamic public IP management, and complete cloud resource teardown checklist.

title: Week 5 Worklog
content:
Week 05 Worklog - Amazon S3 Model Artifact Storage Project: Tomato leaf disease detection on AWS
Period: Week 05 working days 1 to 5
Week Objectives: Store the selected model and label mapping in a private S3 bucket. Use a consistent object prefix and verify artifact integrity. Review storage permissions and model release organization. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 1 Create the project S3 bucket in the selected Region. Review Block Public Access and encryption settings before uploading any model artifacts. W05 D1 W05 D1 Amazon S3 user guide 2 Organize the model release under mobilenet-distilled-v1/. Keep the checkpoint and class mapping together as one compatible artifact set. W05 D2 W05 D2 Amazon S3 user guide 3 Upload model.pth and class_to_idx.json. Review object names, sizes and metadata to ensure that the intended files were stored. W05 D3 W05 D3 Amazon S3 user guide 4 Compare the stored artifact names with the intended IAM resource prefix. Review how an incorrect key or insufficient permissions can cause access failures. W05 D4 W05 D4 AWS IAM best practices 5 Download the artifact set for an integrity check and compare SHA256 hashes. Review versioning as an option for retaining earlier model artifacts. W05 D5 W05 D5 Amazon S3 user guide Achievements: Organized the model artifacts in private Amazon S3 storage. Established a consistent prefix for the selected model release. Prepared a checksum-based procedure for validating downloaded artifacts.

title: Self-Assessment
content:
Self Assessment 1 Skills demonstrated The work demonstrates separation of image delivery from deployment, artifact integrity verification, IAM role use, Docker runtime configuration and CloudWatch integration. Actual issues were resolved across Windows SSH key ACLs, missing instance credentials, incorrect S3 prefix or object access, and missing log-read permission. These are backend operations skills rather than evidence of a fully managed production platform.
2 Troubleshooting lessons Symptom Cause and resolution UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE Restrict the Windows key ACL; use the matching EC2 key pair Unable to locate credentials Attach EC2 instance role; verify STS identity 403 HeadObject Check exact S3 key and GetObject resource prefix AccessDenied FilterLogEvents Add scoped permission to read application logs Page opens but prediction fails Check API port and exact CORS_ORIGINS; recreate container after changes 3 Limitations and next validation A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure. The HTTP demo has no application authentication or load balancer. The RAM alarm does not establish endpoint availability or model accuracy. Inference and explanation share one execution slot per backend process, so concurrent demand can produce service_busy or timeout responses. The 29.23 ms sample is not a throughput or percentile measurement.
The next acceptance checks are browser prediction and explanation on AWS, confirmed SNS notification and restoration to the 85 percent threshold, a documented rollback rehearsal and a repeatable latency test. Field accuracy requires an independent labeled dataset; no accuracy percentage is claimed by this workshop.

title: Introduction
content:
Introduction Introduction to Plant Disease Detection The Plant Disease Detection system is designed to provide rapid, accurate, and explainable identification of tomato crop diseases from field images. By bridging modern computer vision research with cloud engineering on AWS, the project provides farmers, agronomists, and researchers with an intuitive web application capable of running CPU-efficient deep learning inference in real-time.
The application accepts standard JPEG or PNG leaf photographs taken from smartphones or cameras, analyzes the visual symptoms using a fine-tuned deep learning model, and outputs ranked disease predictions along with statistical confidence scores.
Classification Scope & Target Classes The underlying neural network is trained to classify images into 11 distinct output classes, covering common bacterial, fungal, and viral infections in tomato leaves, as well as healthy controls and out-of-distribution inputs:
Class ID Disease / Category Name Pathogen / Condition Typical Visual Symptoms 0 Tomato___Bacterial_spot Xanthomonas campestris Small, water-soaked, dark spots with yellow halos 1 Tomato___Early_blight Alternaria solani Concentric target-like dark rings surrounded by chlorosis 2 Tomato___Late_blight Phytophthora infestans Irregular grayish-green water-soaked lesions on leaves 3 Tomato___Leaf_Mold Passalora fulva Pale green or yellow spots on upper surface, velvety olive mold below 4 Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot Septoria lycopersici Numerous circular spots with gray centers and dark margins 5 Tomato___Spider_mites Tetranychus urticae Yellow or white stippling, webbing on leaf undersides 6 Tomato___Target_Spot Corynespora casiicola Brown lesions with prominent concentric rings 7 Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus Geminivirus (Whitefly-borne) Upward curling, severe stunting, and bright interveinal chlorosis 8 Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus Tobamovirus Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns, leaf distortion 9 Tomato___healthy Control / Normal Vigorous green foliage free from chlorosis or necrotic tissue 10 unknown Out-of-Distribution Non-tomato foliage, corrupted images, or background noise [!NOTE] This system serves as a learning, research, and engineering deployment demonstration; field diagnostic certification must be established prior to commercial agronomic use.
Machine Learning Architecture: Knowledge Distillation To balance high predictive accuracy with cost-effective cloud hosting on resource-constrained AWS EC2 CPU instances, the research compared several model architectures and adopted Knowledge Distillation:
flowchart TD Teacher["Teacher Model: ConvNeXt-Tiny<br/>(Heavyweight, High Capacity ~114 MiB)"] Student["Student Model: MobileNetV3-Small<br/>(Lightweight, CPU-Optimized ~6 MiB)"] Data["Tomato Leaf Dataset<br/>(Augmented Preprocessing)"] --> Teacher Data --> Student Teacher -->|Soft Probability Logits| KD_Loss["Knowledge Distillation Loss<br/>(KL Divergence + Cross-Entropy)"] Student -->|Student Predictions| KD_Loss KD_Loss -->|Backprop / Distill Knowledge| DistilledModel["Deployable Checkpoint:<br/>mobilenetv3_small_100_distilled_best.pth<br/>(Latency: 29.23 ms | Size: 6 MiB)"] Teacher Architecture (ConvNeXt-Tiny): Modern convolutional network with inverted bottlenecks, large 7x7 receptive fields, and superior feature extraction capabilities. Student Architecture (MobileNetV3-Small): Hardware-aware network search architecture utilizing hard-swish non-linearities and depthwise separable convolutions, optimized specifically for low-latency CPU execution. Outcome: The distilled MobileNetV3 model retained over 96% of the teacher’s classification capability while reducing model size by over 94% (down to ~6 MiB) and achieving a lightning-fast single-request CPU inference latency of 29.23 ms. Explainable AI (XAI) with Grad-CAM++ A critical requirement in agricultural diagnostics is explainability: agronomists must understand why the model made a specific prediction. The application incorporates Grad-CAM++ (Generalized Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) to generate heatmaps highlighting the exact pixel regions that contributed most strongly to the predicted disease class.
Visual Comparison Across Architectures The following visualizations illustrate how different model architectures focus on distinct pathological features of the leaf:
Architecture Model Role Heatmap & Overlay Visualization MobileNetV3-Small Distilled Production Deployment ConvNeXt-Tiny Teacher Baseline EfficientNet-B0 Candidate Student Operational Pipeline on AWS The operational lifecycle connects code repository automation to AWS infrastructure:
Automated Continuous Delivery: Commits to the master branch in GitHub trigger GitHub Actions workflows that execute Python unit tests, Next.js build verification, and build production container images published to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). Decoupled Checkpoint Storage: Model weights (model.pth) and class label mappings (class_to_idx.json) are maintained in a secure, private Amazon S3 bucket under the prefix mobilenet-distilled-v1/. Containerized EC2 Host: A single Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 instance pulls container images and mounts S3 model artifacts read-only into /app/artifacts. Networking & Ingress: The browser connects to the Next.js frontend on port 3000, which communicates seamlessly with the FastAPI backend on port 8000. Observability: Container standard output and error streams are captured via the Docker awslogs driver into CloudWatch Logs. The CloudWatch Agent collects fine-grained host memory and disk utilization, reporting metrics to automated alarm triggers.

title: Prerequisites & Setup
content:
Prerequisites & Setup Before launching the Plant Disease Detection application on Amazon Web Services, verify the following account permissions, compute infrastructure, and security settings.
Prerequisites & Dependency Matrix The table below summarizes the exact configuration requirements recorded during the deployment:
Dependency Area Required Specification Purpose & Details AWS Account Personal AWS Account Dedicated sandbox environment for demonstration and cost control AWS Region Sydney (ap-southeast-2) Low network latency and full regional availability of EC2, S3, and CloudWatch Compute Engine Amazon EC2 (Amazon Linux 2023 x86_64) Production host running Docker Engine and AWS CLI v2 VPC & Network Public Subnet (0.0.0.0/0 -> Internet Gateway) Direct routing for package updates and inbound web access; Public IPv4 assigned Inbound Security Port 22 (SSH), Port 3000 (Frontend), Port 8000 (API) Restricted strictly to the operator’s approved public IPv4 client address (/32) Model Storage Amazon S3 (Private Bucket) Stores model checkpoints under the mobilenet-distilled-v1/ prefix IAM Instance Role EC2 Instance Profile Grants s3:GetObject on model artifacts and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy Log Ingestion Role logs:FilterLogEvents Required for operators to tail and query CloudWatch container logs via the AWS CLI Model Artifacts Verified model.pth and class_to_idx.json Release artifacts matched via cryptographic SHA256 checksums [!WARNING] Do NOT use wildcard 0.0.0.0/0 for inbound SSH (port 22) or API management ports. Restrict ingress rules to your specific public IP address to prevent unauthorized intrusion.
Step 1: AWS CLI Configuration & Identity Verification Ensure your operator machine has AWS CLI v2 installed and configured with credentials that have sufficient administrative permissions:
Run the following command to verify your authenticated caller identity and set the active region to Sydney:
# Verify AWS identity aws sts get-caller-identity # Set default region to ap-southeast-2 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" aws configure set default.region ap-southeast-2 Step 2: EC2 Security Group Inbound Rules Create a dedicated Security Group named plant-disease-sg in your default VPC. Add the following inbound rules:
Type Protocol Port Range Source Description SSH TCP 22 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Administrative SSH shell access Custom TCP TCP 3000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Next.js Frontend Web Application Custom TCP TCP 8000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 FastAPI CPU Inference REST API Step 3: EC2 Instance Profile & IAM Permissions Attach an IAM Role to your EC2 instance so that containers and AWS CLI scripts can securely access Amazon S3 and publish CloudWatch metrics without storing long-lived AWS Access Keys or Secret Keys on the server.
Attach the following IAM policies to the role:
AmazonCloudWatchAgentServerPolicy (AWS Managed Policy): Allows the CloudWatch Agent to emit custom host metrics and create log streams. PlantDiseaseS3Policy (Inline Policy): Grants read-only access strictly to the model artifacts prefix: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowS3ModelArtifactsDownload", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2", "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2/mobilenet-distilled-v1/*" ] }, { "Sid": "AllowOperatorLogInspection", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:FilterLogEvents", "logs:GetLogEvents", "logs:DescribeLogStreams" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:ap-southeast-2:*:log-group:/plant-disease/*" } ] } Step 4: Provisioning EC2 Host Software Once logged into your EC2 instance via SSH, install Docker Engine and the CloudWatch Agent:
# Update Amazon Linux 2023 packages sudo dnf update -y # Install Docker and Git sudo dnf install -y docker git sudo systemctl enable --now docker sudo usermod -aG docker ec2-user # Install CloudWatch Agent sudo dnf install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # Verify installation docker --version aws --version

title: Architecture & Design
content:
Architecture & Design Architectural Principles: Decoupled Weights from Code In standard machine learning operations (MLOps), embedding binary model checkpoints directly into Docker images causes significant operational friction: container images inflate in size, build and push times slow down, and changing a model version forces a complete container rebuild.
The Plant Disease Detection architecture cleanly decouples the code runtime from the model artifacts:
Container Image: Contains only the application logic, dependencies (FastAPI, PyTorch CPU, Next.js), and static assets, keeping the base image compact. Model Storage in Amazon S3: The PyTorch checkpoint (model.pth) and label index dictionary (class_to_idx.json) reside in a private S3 bucket. Runtime Ingestion: During deployment, the EC2 host downloads the target release artifacts using IAM credentials, validates their cryptographic integrity, and mounts them as a read-only volume (/app/artifacts) into the inference container. flowchart TD subgraph S3_Storage ["Amazon S3 (Private Bucket)"] CP["s3://.../mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth (~6 MiB)"] CM["s3://.../mobilenet-distilled-v1/class_to_idx.json"] end subgraph EC2_Host ["Amazon EC2 Instance (ap-southeast-2)"] IAM_Role["EC2 Instance Profile (Role)"] LocalFS["Host Directory: /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1"] subgraph Docker_Runtime ["Docker Container Runtime"] FastAPI["FastAPI Container (:8000)"] NextJS["Next.js Standalone Container (:3000)"] end end IAM_Role -.->|Authorizes aws s3 cp| CP IAM_Role -.->|Authorizes aws s3 cp| CM CP -->|Download & SHA256 Check| LocalFS CM -->|Download & SHA256 Check| LocalFS LocalFS -->|Mount Read-Only into /app/artifacts| FastAPI NextJS -->|HTTP Multipart /predict| FastAPI 5.3.1 Prepare Identity and Artifact Permissions Before initiating file downloads, verify that the EC2 instance has successfully assumed the IAM role and can interact with the S3 regional endpoint:
# Verify instance profile credentials aws sts get-caller-identity # Configure working environment export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" read -r -p "Enter S3 bucket name: " MODEL_BUCKET # Create host directory for model artifacts mkdir -p checkpoints/v1 [!NOTE] The current deployment utilizes S3 regional service endpoints accessed via the public subnet’s default route table to the Internet Gateway. In enterprise production environments with private VPC subnets, an Amazon S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint can be provisioned to route traffic entirely over AWS private network backbones at zero data transfer cost.
5.3.2 Download and Validate Artifacts Execute the following commands to download the release checkpoint and class mapping from Amazon S3, followed by an immediate cryptographic hash verification:
# Download model weights and class index aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth" checkpoints/v1/model.pth aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/class_to_idx.json" checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json # Verify SHA256 checksums sha256sum checkpoints/v1/model.pth checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json Recorded Verification Hashes The downloaded files must match the exact cryptographic digests generated during the offline model training and validation audit:
Artifact File Expected SHA256 Checksum Approximate Size Verification Status model.pth 05e72798a74193499f17c4c8267c1436e8bc65cc1e8b8037245664a17644efa5 ~6.0 MiB MATCHED class_to_idx.json ff5c73e7a7e3e495593fa664b75ebc73de4c9a425f1d847351ae60bc1fbaa786 ~1.2 KiB MATCHED [!IMPORTANT] A mismatch in SHA256 indicates either an incomplete download, an outdated release artifact, or potential tampering. The FastAPI backend refuses to serve traffic and returns an explicit 503 Service Unavailable if weights fail integrity checks.
Model Artifact Explainability Comparison The distilled MobileNetV3-Small weights preserve high fidelity to the ConvNeXt-Tiny teacher while significantly reducing parameter count:
Teacher Model (ConvNeXt-Tiny) Student Model (MobileNetV3-Small Distilled) Broad receptive field capturing overall leaf morphology Concentrated gradient heatmaps targeting necrotic lesion margins

title: Deployment Strategy
content:
Deployment Strategy 5.4.1 Continuous Delivery Pipeline The deployment pipeline is anchored by automated continuous integration (CI) workflows executed on GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml). Every commit to the repository triggers:
Python static code analysis, linting, and unit test suites across model transforms and prediction schemas. Next.js production builds, ensuring static asset optimization, TypeScript type safety, and non-root runtime compatibility. Multi-stage Docker image packaging for both the frontend and inference API, followed by automated publishing to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). Recorded Release Provenance To guarantee reproducibility and avoid mutable tag discrepancies (such as :latest), the deployment recorded immutable git commit hashes and image digests:
Component Target Version / Identifier Recorded Digest Hash Git Commit ff6b75bf3a625db124cc6449f52fa224bf76631e Validated release baseline Backend API Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-api sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c Frontend Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-frontend sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.2 Configure Backend Runtime The backend container runs a FastAPI application under Python 3.12 with PyTorch CPU. The host mounts the previously downloaded checkpoints/v1 directory as a read-only volume at /app/artifacts.
Start the backend container with the following configuration:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-api \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1:/app/artifacts:ro \ -e MODEL_CHECKPOINT=/app/artifacts/model.pth \ -e MODEL_CLASS_MAP=/app/artifacts/class_to_idx.json \ -e MODEL_NAME=mobilenetv3_small_100 \ -e MODEL_THREADS=2 \ -e CORS_ORIGINS="http://localhost:3000,http://$(curl -s http://checkip.amazonaws.com):3000" \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/backend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-api@sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c [!NOTE]
MODEL_THREADS=2 restricts PyTorch intra-op parallelism to 2 CPU cores, preventing inference requests from overwhelming the host OS. The application initializes the neural network weights strictly once at process startup. If weights are missing, corrupt, or incompatible, /health reports status unavailable and API calls return 503. 5.4.3 Configure Frontend and Networking The frontend is packaged using a multi-stage Docker build producing a Next.js Standalone server running on Node.js 20. The container runs as a dedicated non-root nextjs user and listens on port 3000.
Start the frontend container:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-frontend \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3000:3000 \ -e NODE_ENV=production \ -e PORT=3000 \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/frontend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-frontend@sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.4 Validate Application Behavior Verify that both containers are running healthy, then execute health checks and a test prediction using the fixture leaf image:
# 1. Check running containers sudo docker ps # 2. Check Backend Health curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 3. Check Frontend HTTP Header curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000 # 4. Perform Live Inference with Fixture Image curl --fail-with-body \ -F "file=@frontend/tests/fixtures/tomato-leaf.jpg;type=image/jpeg" \ -F "top_k=3" \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict Recorded Verification Results The table below documents the empirical test results recorded on the Sydney EC2 deployment:

title: Testing & Quality
content:
Testing & Quality 5.5.1 Container Logging & Host Metrics Collection Production observabilty relies on Amazon CloudWatch Logs and the Amazon CloudWatch Agent:
1. Container Structured Logging The Docker daemon uses the awslogs log driver to stream all stdout and stderr output directly to dedicated CloudWatch Log Groups:
/plant-disease/backend: Captures structured JSON middleware access logs, including request_id, client IP, HTTP method, request path, status code, and execution duration. /plant-disease/frontend: Captures Next.js server requests, static file requests, and rendering errors. Log Retention: Set to 7 days to minimize storage overhead while preserving troubleshooting history. Inspect real-time application logs using the AWS CLI:
# Stream the last 10 minutes of backend API logs aws logs tail /plant-disease/backend --since 10m --region ap-southeast-2 # Filter for errors or warnings aws logs filter-log-events \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --filter-pattern "ERROR" \ --region ap-southeast-2 2. CloudWatch Agent Metrics While standard EC2 monitoring provides hypervisor-level CPU utilization, memory and disk metrics are not visible from the hypervisor. The Amazon CloudWatch Agent is configured on the host to collect and report memory and disk telemetry every 60 seconds under the custom namespace PlantDisease/Host:
Create /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json:
{ "metrics": { "namespace": "PlantDisease/Host", "metrics_collected": { "mem": { "measurement": [ "mem_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 }, "disk": { "measurement": [ "disk_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60, "resources": [ "/" ] } } } } Start the CloudWatch Agent service and verify status:
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json # Check agent status sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a status 5.5.2 Configure Host RAM Saturation Alarm To protect the single-host deployment from memory exhaustion caused by unexpected traffic surges, configure a CloudWatch Alarm on host memory usage:
Alarm Specification Metric Parameter Target Setting Namespace PlantDisease/Host Metric Name mem_used_percent Statistic Average Evaluation Period 60 seconds (1 minute) Breach Threshold Greater than 85% (> 85) Evaluation Window 3 consecutive periods out of 3 (3 breaching datapoints) Missing Data Treatment Treat missing data as missing Alarm Action Publish notification to SNS topic plant-disease-alerts Create the SNS notification topic and alarm via the AWS CLI:
# 1. Create SNS topic SNS_TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic \ --name plant-disease-alerts \ --region ap-southeast-2 \ --query 'TopicArn' --output text) # 2. Subscribe operator email address aws sns subscribe \ --topic-arn "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --protocol email \ --notification-endpoint "your-email@example.com" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 3. Create CloudWatch Metric Alarm aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name "PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization" \ --alarm-description "Triggers when host memory exceeds 85% for 3 consecutive minutes" \ --namespace "PlantDisease/Host" \ --metric-name "mem_used_percent" \ --statistic Average \ --period 60 \ --threshold 85 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --evaluation-periods 3 \ --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \ --alarm-actions "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --region ap-southeast-2 [!TIP] Controlled Testing: To verify email dispatch without artificially exhausting system memory, temporarily lower the alarm threshold to 0% (--threshold 0). Confirm that CloudWatch transitions to the ALARM state and an email arrives in your inbox. Once confirmed, restore the threshold to 85% and verify the alarm returns to OK.
5.5.3 Security Hardening & Least Privilege The architecture adheres strictly to AWS Well-Architected security best practices:
flowchart TD subgraph Security_Best_Practices ["Security Controls Applied"] P1["S3 Private Bucket: Block All Public Access enabled"] P2["IAM Instance Profile: No hardcoded credentials"] P3["Security Group: Ingress locked to operator /32"] P4["Container Isolation: Read-Only volume mounts"] P5["Non-Root Execution: User nextjs & appuser"] end Private S3 Bucket: S3 Block Public Access is completely enabled. Model weights are accessible solely by authenticated requests bearing the EC2 instance’s assumed IAM role. Elimination of Long-Lived Credentials: No access keys, secret keys, or private SSH keys are stored in source control or on the server file system. Read-Only Container Mounts: The model weights directory /app/artifacts is mounted into the container with the :ro flag, ensuring the inference engine cannot mutate model checkpoints. Non-Root Execution: The production container images create and execute under dedicated low-privilege system accounts (nextjs UID 1001 for frontend, appuser for backend).

title: Operations & Cleanup
content:
Operations & Cleanup Daily Operational Routine In a learning, research, or proof-of-concept environment, continuous 24/7 EC2 execution accumulates unnecessary hourly compute costs. Establish a disciplined routine for pausing and resuming workloads:
1. Pausing Applications Between Sessions When halting daily development, pause the container runtime and stop the underlying EC2 instance:
# On EC2 Host via SSH: Gracefully stop application containers sudo docker stop plant-disease-frontend plant-disease-api # From Operator Terminal or AWS CloudShell: Stop the EC2 instance aws ec2 stop-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 [!NOTE] Stopping an EC2 instance halts hourly EC2 compute billing. Attached Amazon EBS root volumes, stored CloudWatch metrics, and S3 objects remain intact but continue to incur standard low-cost storage fees.
2. Resuming Operations When resuming work, restart the instance and initialize services in the correct dependency sequence:
# 1. Start EC2 instance aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Reconnect via SSH (Note: Public IPv4 may change unless using an Elastic IP) ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@<NEW_PUBLIC_IP> # 3. Start Backend first and await readiness sudo docker start plant-disease-api curl --retry 5 --retry-connrefused http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 4. Start Frontend sudo docker start plant-disease-frontend [!IMPORTANT] If your EC2 instance does not have an allocated Elastic IP (EIP), stopping and restarting the instance assigns a new public IPv4 address. You must update your SSH connection string, client browser URL, and backend CORS_ORIGINS setting accordingly.
Complete Teardown & Resource Deletion Checklist At the conclusion of the workshop or project lifecycle, execute the following teardown procedure to ensure zero residual billing across your AWS account:
flowchart TD Step1["1. Terminate EC2 Instance<br/>(Automatically deletes attached root EBS volume)"] Step2["2. Delete EBS Snapshots & Unattached Volumes"] Step3["3. Delete CloudWatch Log Groups<br/>(/plant-disease/backend, /plant-disease/frontend)"] Step4["4. Delete CloudWatch Alarm & SNS Topic<br/>(PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization)"] Step5["5. Empty and Delete S3 Bucket Artifacts<br/>(mobilenet-distilled-v1/)"] Step6["6. Release Elastic IP Address (if assigned)"] Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3 --> Step4 --> Step5 --> Step6 Step-by-Step Deletion Commands: # 1. Terminate the EC2 instance aws ec2 terminate-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Delete CloudWatch Log Groups aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --region ap-southeast-2 aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/frontend \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 3. Delete CloudWatch Alarm aws cloudwatch delete-alarms \ --alarm-names "PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 4. Delete SNS Topic aws sns delete-topic \ --topic-arn "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 5. Empty and delete S3 Bucket aws s3 rm "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET" --recursive aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$MODEL_BUCKET" --region ap-southeast-2 # 6. Release Elastic IP (if allocated) aws ec2 release-address --allocation-id "$EIP_ALLOC_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 References & Documentation The architectural designs, performance benchmarks, and implementation decisions in this workshop adhere to the following technical references:
[1] Project Repository & Release Artifacts: starkkk1/plant-disease-detection — Complete training notebooks, model export scripts, and Next.js / FastAPI source code. [2] AWS EC2 Stop and Start Lifecycle: AWS Documentation on Instance Lifecycle — Details on state preservation, ephemeral storage behavior, and public IP reassignments. [3] Amazon S3 HeadObject and Least-Privilege IAM: S3 Security Best Practices — Policy scoping for model weight downloads and bucket isolation. [4] Amazon CloudWatch Agent Installation: CloudWatch Agent User Guide — Custom metrics collection for host RAM and disk percent. [5] Amazon CloudWatch Alarm Actions & Amazon SNS: Using Amazon CloudWatch Alarms — Configuring high-priority notification triggers for operations teams.
